newsitem.title: NORWAY: FEATURE - Norway coastal cruise may sail into dire straits.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Norway coastal cruise may sail into dire straits.

text.p: For more than a hundred years, Norway's romantic Hurtigruta passenger ships have cruised the scenic coast to the Arctic north and back.
But for all its sights and legendary reputation, the cruise is a loss-making business. The ships could well sail into dire straits once state subsidies run out six years from now.
The Hurtigruta, or Coastal Express, was inaugurated in 1893 when sea lanes were the quickest way of getting from one point to another in Norway.
Planes and other modern means of transport have since taken over and Coastal Express passengers nowadays are mostly tourists who come to admire the jagged mountains and deep fjords.
"Some travellers return year after year," said captain Kjell Skjoldvaer of MS Lofoten, built in 1966 and one of the fleet's oldest ships.
"The enthusiasts, many of them Swiss or German, prefer to travel during the low season when it is less crowded and prices are lower. Some even spend Christmas on board."

Last century, with only 28 lighthouses dotting the rough coastline north of Trondheim and with only two charts of the area in existence, no one was willing to run the risk of regular sailing in the wild waters off north Norway.
Two of the country's leading steamship companies turned down a request from the government to start the Coastal Express.
It was only after the government agreed to split the costs that Captain Richard With of the newly-founded Vesteraalens Dampskibsselskab steamship company took up the challenge.

In 1990, however, authorities said that 100 years of subsidiies was more than enough but backed down following loud protests from the coastal population. Parliament eventually gave the Coastal Express a flat 1.9 billion Norwegian crowns ($296 million), and told shipowners to break even in 11 years.

"From the year 2002 we are on our own," said Steinar Saetherdal, marketing director at Ofoten and Vesteraalens Dampskibsselskap (OVDS). "We decided to build the new ships as big as possible in order to bring down costs per passenger."
Together, the two Coastal Express companies, OVDS and Troms Fylkes Dampskipsselskap (TFDS), have invested around three billion crowns in new ships, doubling passenger capacity.
But the Coastal Express is still about 200 million crowns a year away from making a profit, and no one is willing to say the future looks bright.
Critics have accused the Coastal Express of being overpriced, and passenger numbers declined to 331,000 in 1995 from 363,000 in 1994. Activity, however, picked up in the first half of this year.

Saeterdahl said the companies had to take several aspects into consideration to meet the challenges. Sailing distances of up to 1,550 miles, the number of ports the ships dock at and prices are core issues to be dealt with.
"I think we will manage, but it is not going to be an easy job," said Saetherdahl.
Three generations of ships are in operation today -- traditional ships built in the 1960s, a mid-generation from the 1980s and new modern ships built this decade.

Most travellers prefer more comfort than the traditional ships can offer. Passengers on the modern ships sip long drinks in the upper-deck conservatory, watching the changing scenery along one of the most spectacular coastlines in the world.
The route passes through magnificent fjord landscapes and stunning mountain ranges and the ships' architecture reveals that the scenery is the main atttraction.

The main feature is the observation lounge at the forward end of the superstructure, a glazed atrium extending down three deck levels and a panorama lounge bar. There are no discos and passengers are not cajoled into playing deck games or participating in aerobic classes.
But some enthusiasts stick to the traditional ships.

"We prefer the old ships. There is no alternative for us," said Kurt Althoehn, a German teacher from Kaiserslautern travelling with his wife. "We had to take this journey now. In a few years the old ships could be gone forever."

The traditional black-and-white ships have earned a reputation for reliability regardless of the weather. But these days the ships, once the backbone of the transport system, are sadly obsolete and unable to make a profit even at the best of times. For every ten crowns earned, 15 are lost.
Officials said it is paramount that not only tourists go on the cruise but that many local Norwegians continue to travel by boat the old way rather than catching a flight or a train.

"The companies should never try to turn the Coastal Express in to a full-blown cruise product," said Boerre Berglund, a director at the Norwegian Tourist Board's German branch. ($1=6.419 Norwegian Crown)
